items.title: 15 old-school casserole recipes that feel like home for boomers and Gen Xers
items.summary:
Childhood dishes can take you straight back to your seat at the family dinner table. Comfort meals that were served there are uber-nostalgic. And there is one dish that represents the epitome of Gen X and baby boomer childhoods: casseroles.

These one-dish wonders were loaded with flavor and baked to perfection. Pulled straight from the oven to the dinner table, casseroles filled the house with the smell of unique home-cooked recipes.

And while most of us are eating casseroles today at Thanksgiving , Gen Xers and boomers grew up eating casseroles on the reg.

Here are 15 old-school casserole recipes that Redditors grew up eating, which are just as yummy today:

Chicken casseroles 

Fancy Fast Chicken casserole 

“ Fancy Fast Chicken is delicious and so simple. Line up chicken breasts in a casserole dish. Dump uncooked stuffing over top the chicken breasts. Pour Cream of Mushroom (Onion or chicken works too) and incorporate it into the stuffing. Top with cheese of your choice, and fried onions if you’re inclined. Bake at 350 for 45min or until chicken is thoroughly cooked.” – Applepoisoneer 

Chicken Curry Divan casserole 

“My favorite is Chicken Curry Divan. A friend made it for me in college 40 years ago and it is a favorite to this day. Never disappoints. Many people have asked me for the recipe over the years. My best friends kids now that they are grown have each approached me for it.

1 1/2 lbs chicken breast tenders cooked and cut into bite sized pieces
3 cups broccoli in bite sized pieces
2 cans Cream of Chicken soup
1 cup mayonnaise (must be Mayo)

items.t: 15 old-school casserole recipes that feel like home for boomers and Gen Xers

items.title: Vet demonstrates ‘squish the cat’ method of safe cat handling in delightfully helpful video
items.summary:
If you’ve ever tried to make a cat do something it doesn’t want to do, you’ve likely experienced the terror that a cat’s wrath can invoke. Our cute, cuddly feline friends may be small, but the razor blades on their feet are no joke when they decide to utilize them. Even cats who love us can get spicy if we try to manhandle them , so we can imagine how things will go with cats who don’t know us well. But sometimes it’s necessary to handle a cat even if it’s resistant to the idea.

This is where Vancouver veterinarian Dr. Uri Burstyn comes in. His “How to pick up a cat like a pro” video , in which he demonstrates a few ways of picking up and handling a cat, has been viewed over 23 million times since he shared it in 2018. Unlike many viral videos, it’s not humorous and nothing outrageous happens, but the combo of Burstyn’s calm demeanor and his repeated instructions to “squish that cat” has endeared him to the masses .

The video truly is helpful; he shows the ways to pick up a cat that make them feel the most secure using his cats, Claudia (then 1 year old) and Mr. Pirate (then 14). He explains that cats spook very easily and it’s best to introduce yourself to them gently. Let them sniff your fingers, keeping your fingers curled in, and once they’ve sniffed you, you can often give them a light rub on the cheek or under the chin.

Why cats scratch when you pick them up 

Picking them up is a different story. The reason many cats will claw or scratch you when you try to pick them up is because they feel unsupported or unsafe , so they’ll scramble around trying to get some…
items.t: Vet demonstrates ‘squish the cat’ method of safe cat handling in delightfully helpful video

items.title: 6th grader’s science fair project answers age-old question: ‘Do cat buttholes touch everything?’
items.summary:
Cat owners are a special breed of people. Sometimes, in dealing with feline friends , they have unique questions that even Google doesn’t always have the answer to. This is probably the sole reason cat forums exist, but one kid who needed a 6th grade science project decided to skip the cat forums for answers and instead use the scientific method. Kaeden Henry, then a sixth grader living in Florida, bravely pondered a question few (if any) have been brave enough to ask: do cat buttholes touch every surface they sit on?

Since cats do whatever the heck they want , training them not to jump on kitchen counters is a feat even Hercules struggles to complete. These fierce felines don’t care if you’re cooking dinner or trying to get comfy in bed. If they want to sit somewhere, they’re going to do it. The thought of cat butts on that expensive Serta pillow designed to feel like you’re sleeping on a cloud can gross people out, but thanks to Kaeden, you no longer have to wonder if the butthole itself is also making contact.

The scientific method as it was meant to be used. Courtesy of Kerry Hyde

items.title: A juice company dumped orange peels in a national park. This is what it looks like today.
items.summary:
In 1997, ecologists Daniel Janzen and Winnie Hallwachs approached an orange juice company in Costa Rica called Del Oro with an off-the-wall idea . In exchange for donating a portion of unspoiled, forested land to the Área de Conservación Guanacaste, a nature preserve in the country’s northwest, the park would allow the company to dump its discarded orange peels and pulp, free of charge, in a heavily grazed, largely deforested area nearby.

One year later, one thousand trucks poured into the national park, offloading over 12,000 metric tons of sticky, mealy, orange compost onto the worn-out plot. The project was forced to end after just its second year, though, when rival juice manufacturer TicoFrut sued Del Oro, alleging it had defiled a national park, and Costa Rica’s Supreme Court ultimately sided with the plaintiff. The site was left untouched and largely unexamined for over a decade.

Finding the site years later on 

Sixteen years later, Janzen dispatched graduate student Timothy Treuer to look for the site where the food waste was dumped.

Treuer initially set out to locate the large placard that marked the plot, and failed.

The first deposit of orange peels in 1997. Photo by Dan Janzen. 

“It’s a huge sign, bright yellow lettering. We should have been able to see it,” Treuer says. After wandering around for half an hour with no luck, he consulted Janzen, who gave him more detailed instructions on how to find the plot.

When he returned a week later and confirmed he was in the right place, Treuer was floored. Compared to the adjacent barren former pastureland, the…
items.t: A juice company dumped orange peels in a national park. This is what it looks like today.

items.title: Kieran Culkin says his wife’s very British hot take on the ‘useless’ American top sheet blew his mind

The differences between European culture and American culture never cease to surprise (and entertain) us. From toilet preferences to personality traits , Americans do many things in distinct ways. 

And actor Kieran Culkin recently shared a funny cultural realization that happened between him and his British wife, Jazz Charton. 

In a new interview with JOE , Culkin was asked about Charton’s “Britishisms”. And he opened up about one major difference between British and American bedrooms that surprised him.

Kieran Culkin says he thought his British wife was lying when she told him people in England don't use top sheets on their beds

"There's also things that she'll say it's because of where she's from. And I'm like, I actually don't know if you're just saying this or if this is… pic.twitter.com/1QSbiWaCDd 

— Casper (@CasperOnChain) November 22, 2026 

The surprising American bedroom habit 

During the sit-down interview with JOE , Culkin shared that there’s “always some new thing” that Charton points out is odd to her about American culture. Most recently, it was something in American bedrooms.

“She hates a [top] sheet on a bed,” he explained. “She’s like, ‘It should [just] be a duvet. In England, we only do the duvet. We don’t do the sheet’.”

At first, he didn’t see her point—but then he did.

“So I thought, she was full of sh*t!” he added. “She kept saying, ‘Why are these always bunched up? Why are they always tossed up? They’re on the floor.’ She goes, ‘Cuz we don’t have these in England. It’s a stupid f*cking thing in a bed.’ And then I’ve since asked, and…

items.title: The actor who played the Fonz couldn’t easily read the scripts. He found his own way through.
items.summary:
Henry Winkler spent 11 seasons playing one of television’s coolest characters. Originally given a minor role on Happy Days , Arthur Fonzarelli became one of the show’s biggest stars. As confident as the Fonz appeared on screen, some of Winkler’s most uncomfortable moments came before the cameras even started rolling.

As Winkler explained in a 2023 interview with PBS NewsHour , he struggled to read scripts because of dyslexia , a learning disability he wasn’t diagnosed with until he was 31. By then, Winkler had developed his own techniques for getting through auditions and learning his lines.

Henry Winkler on stage at 2018 Supercon. Photo Credit: Super Festivals/ Wikimedia Commons/ CC BY 2.0 (cropped) 

How Henry Winkler got through his auditions 

Winkler graduated from the Yale School of Drama in 1970 with a master’s degree, but getting through auditions presented a particular challenge.

Actors are often asked to read unfamiliar material during an audition. For Winkler, this meant demonstrating his ability to play a character while struggling to read the dialogue.

Speaking to The Yale Center for Dyslexia & Creativity , he explained how he would quickly memorize as much of the script as possible and improvise the portions he couldn’t remember.

“You learn to negotiate with your learning challenge,” said Winkler. “I could instantly memorize a lot of it and then what I didn’t know, I made up and threw caution to the wind and did it with conviction and sometimes I made them laugh and sometimes I got hired,” he added.

items.t: The actor who played the Fonz couldn’t easily read the scripts. He found his own way through.

items.title: How this ‘harsh parenting rule’ helped save 99.8 percent of people during a historic tsunami
items.summary:
Most of us, who have ever traveled on an airplane, are familiar with the notion of securing our safety before we secure the safety of those around us. A flight attendant often stands in the aisle and says some variation of: “Always put on your own oxygen mask first before assisting others.” We hear this sentence so often that many tune out. But its sentiment is essential: you can’t help others if you, yourself, are in peril.

The concept in Japan is known as Tsunami-tendenko. As explained in a research paper by Susumu Cato and Ken Oshitani for National Library of Medicine , it’s a guide that applies to all. “‘Tsunami-tendenko,’ a guideline suggesting that individuals prioritize their own safety over aiding others during large-scale disasters.”

Putting one’s self first 

The concept, according to Japanese newspaper The Mainichi isn’t known by everyone. “‘Tsunami tendenko,’ which come from the Tohoku dialect, means, ‘If a tsunami hits, each person should evacuate immediately on their own without caring about others, including their family.’ 

They further explain the origin. “The words were put together in 1990 by late tsunami researcher Fumio Yamashita, a native of Ofunato, Iwate Prefecture, who survived the 1933 Showa Great Sanriku Tsunami. After the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake, the word has come under the spotlight in tsunami evacuation measure promotions.”

Hard for outsiders to understand

items.t: How this ‘harsh parenting rule’ helped save 99.8 percent of people during a historic tsunami

items.title: A woman loved her baby’s name, but after 5 months she wants to change it to Juliette
items.summary:
Baby name regret is surprisingly common amongst new mothers. A poll by Baby Center found that around 9% of mothers experience it after giving birth . There are many reasons why it happens; the big one is that they choose a name and after the baby arrives, it just doesn’t fit.

Another is that parents feel they never got the name they truly wanted because they had to compromise with a partner. In some cases, parents may love a baby’s name but start having problems when others have trouble pronouncing or spelling it. Baby Center says that in 6% of cases, the moms have had the baby’s name changed legally.

Nearly 1 in 10 moms regret the name they chose for their baby, according to survey https://t.co/iTvwkX6RjG 

— CBS News (@CBSNews) September 7, 2024 

Many who keep the name they don’t like choose to give the baby a nickname, use their middle name, or refer to them by a shortened version of their birth name. Recently, a woman on Reddit shared a story that sparked debate: she loves her baby’s name, Genevieve Elise, but after 5 months wants to change it to Juliette because some people don’t know how to say or spell it.

Why do people have a problem with Genevieve? 

“It didn’t even occur to me how many people would have trouble pronouncing/spelling/even getting used to the name. I mean it’s a pretty established name,” the mother wrote. “Nonetheless, I’ve decided to change it because while I absolutely adore the name, I don’t want to set her up for a lifetime of corrections and people either making fun or having a hard time with her name. I’ve been losing sleep over…

items.title: Gen Xers keep saying they feel 35. A lifespan study puts that number in perspective.
items.summary:
The phrase “age is just a number” is a popular idiom in American culture. When it comes to aging, it’s a cliché that rings true for many who refuse to let their chronological age define who they are.

And Gen Xers are one generation that has really taken it to heart. Gen Xers, those born between 1965 and 1980, are currently 46-61 years old today.

But they’re a generation that doesn’t feel that “old”. Many Gen Xers have reported feeling the magic number of 35 years old.

And science backs them up, according to a study published in the journal Psychonomic Bulletin & Review , where researchers studied 1,470 Danish adult participants between the ages of 20 and 97.

They found that of participants over the age of 40, an impressive 20% reported feeling younger than their chronological age. Translation: Gen Xers today may actually feel that they are 36-48 years old.

Why Gen X feels younger than they are 

What set Gen Xers apart age-wise in the study was their acceptance of a “lifespan-developmental view”. This is defined as a psychological theory that people tend to choose an internal age that they consistently view themselves as, called an “attractor age”.

For study participants, that was deemed to be 25 years old. This age serves as a “psychological anchor” of comparison, likely because at 25, true adulthood begins in terms of many significant aspects of life being established, including career, financial independence, romantic relationships, and the start of families.

While decades may stack on to the age of 25, study participants noted it was still an age they could…
items.t: Gen Xers keep saying they feel 35. A lifespan study puts that number in perspective.

items.title: The City That Kicked Out Cars Before It Was Cool
items.summary:
A s a taxi driver, Juan Barbosa should in theory be one of the strongest opponents of a crackdown on cars. But, puffing on a cigarette beside his vehicle on a sultry August afternoon, the inhabitant of Pontevedra, Spain, admits that he finds himself in something of an existential crisis. 

“As a driver, I suffer,” says Barbosa, who has been ferrying passengers around the northwestern city for two decades. “We can’t enter certain areas unless we have a customer or a booking. We have to take longer routes. But as a pedestrian, life is better. I enjoy it when there are fewer vehicles around.” 

Post-pandemic, pedestrian-first urban planning is now all the rage, from 15-minute cities to low-traffic zones and the rise of soft mobility ( human-powered or low-emission electric transport). But Pontevedra, which is home to 85,000 people in the city and just under a million in the province, was way ahead of the curve. It technically began its war on cars last century. (In 1999, to be precise.) 

The urban transformation of Pontevedra was carried out gradually, over the course of several years. Credit: Peter Yeung 
 Today Pontevedra, which fittingly is located on one of the world-famous Camino de Santiago pilgrimage routes , is considered perhaps the greatest example in the world when it comes to getting rid of cars. Every year, delegations of mayors, professors and city planners make their own pilgrimage to learn about this great vanishing act. 

“Pontevedra is an influential example and something we speak of often,” says Mark Nieuwenhuijsen , director of the urban planning,…
items.t: The City That Kicked Out Cars Before It Was Cool
